# `cap_grant_exceeded`: the program reaches a capability `main` was not granted

`main`'s capability parameters are the program's grant: everything the program
can do, through any chain of calls, must fit inside it. This error points at a
use (a builtin call) that needs a capability outside the grant, and labels each
call on the way from `main` to it. A module's `needs` line does not raise the
grant; it only declares what that module's code may use.

## A program that triggers it

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO.Console
  needs IO.FileWrite

  fn save(n : Int) : () do
    let _ = file_write("/tmp/count", int_to_string(n))
    ()
  end

  fn main(_c : Cap(IO.Console)) do
    save(1)
    println("saved")
  end
end
```

## The fix

Grant `main` the capability too, by adding a parameter for it (or remove the
use):

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO.Console
  needs IO.FileWrite

  fn save(n : Int) : () do
    let _ = file_write("/tmp/count", int_to_string(n))
    ()
  end

  fn main(_c : Cap(IO.Console), _fw : Cap(IO.FileWrite)) do
    save(1)
    println("saved")
  end
end
```

## Why the rule exists

The grant on `main` is what the person running the program agrees to. Reading
`main`'s signature tells them the most the program can do, so a program that
writes files must say so there, however deep the write is.

See also: [the language reference](../capabilities.md).
